etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English gliden, from Old English glīdan, from Proto-West Germanic *glīdan, from Proto-Germanic *glīdaną, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰleydʰ-.

Cognate with West Frisian glide, glydzje, Low German glieden, Dutch glijden, German gleiten, Norwegian Nynorsk gli, Danish glide, Swedish glida, Finnish liitää.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To move softly, smoothly, or effortlessly.

quote.citation: 1807, William Wordsworth, “Composed upon Westminster Bridge, September 3, 1802 (Sonnet 14)”, in Poems, in Two Volumes, volume I, London:  […]  Longman, Hurst, Rees, and Orme, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: The river glideth at his own sweet will:

quote.citation: 1834, L[etitia] E[lizabeth] L[andon], chapter XVII, in Francesca Carrara. […], volume III, London: Richard Bentley, […], (successor to Henry Colburn), →OCLC, page 137:
quote.text: It is odd how easily the common-places of morality or of sentiment glide off in conversation. Well, they are "exceedingly helpful," and so Lord Avonleigh found them.

quote.citation: 1874, Marcus Clarke, For the Term of His Natural Life, Chapter VI:
quote.text: The water over which the boats glided was black and smooth, rising into huge foamless billows, the more terrible because they were silent.
But it was 37-year-old Giggs who looked like a care-free teenager as he glided across the pitch he knows so well to breathtaking effect.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To fly unpowered, as of an aircraft. Also relates to gliding birds and flying fish.

quote.citation: 1947 January and February, O. S. Nock, “"The Aberdonian" in Wartime”, in Railway Magazine, page 8:
quote.text: The tide was out, and we drew up amid the strong bracing smell of seaweed, with gulls screeching, wheeling around, and gliding on the wind.

definitions.definition: (phonetics) To pass with a glide, as the voice.
(phonology) A transitional sound, especially a semivowel.
(fencing) An attack or preparatory movement made by sliding down the opponent’s blade, keeping it in constant contact.
A bird, the glede or kite.
A kind of cap affixed to the base of the legs of furniture to prevent it from damaging the floor while being moved.
The joining of two sounds without a break.
A smooth and sliding step in dancing the waltz.
